Title: Munir : in a lamp
Pitch_Text:
Weakened by years of melancholy, play as Munir, a genie trapped in his lamp, who tries to rebuild the temple of his late companion. Use the weight-based mechanics at your disposal to solve the various puzzles.

Munir is a puzzle adventure game developed around the imposed themes: "unconventional character", "world made of dynamic tiles" and "procedural animation". The game design was entirely built to fully leverage an unusual controller.
SumUp_Text:
During this project, I dedicated a large part of the production to iterating on the physics and the feel of our controller in order to make it as pleasant and intuitive to use as possible. I also took the opportunity to learn tooling and to create custom inspectors.

This project was the first time I was not alone in the programmer role within a team. While remaining the main programmer, I was able to benefit from the help of tech artists, a field I discovered through this experience.

Project completed as part of my studies at Rubika Montréal.
Realisation_Text:
For the first time, I shared the programmer role with tech artists in charge of procedural animation, sound and VFX. As for me, I worked on:

• Controller and 3D physics : The controller, the core feature of our concept, represented the majority of my work. Inspired by "Endoparasitic", our controller translates its essence into a 3D environment: the player grabs onto a surface (such as the ground) and drags themselves from that new anchor point to move.
Extensive research was conducted to make the controller intuitive, responsive and fluid, both in terms of controls and features to implement. How many buttons are needed? Should the hand slide on surfaces or keep a certain distance from the ground, requiring a button to lift it? Should it always seek the lowest point? These were all questions that guided this design phase.
The final controller relies on three inputs: one to grab, one to lift the hand or body, and a joystick to move. The hand stays at a fixed distance from the ground and does not stick to walls. Everything was designed to provide a fast and pleasant learning curve.

• Tooling : To compensate for a short production time, I developed a tool procedurally generating a mesh in the scene from a list of coordinates and a chosen material. It greatly simplified the setup of connections between our actuators (levers, buttons, …) and our receivers (doors, pistons, …). I also created a custom inspector to simplify the management and editing of these elements.

• Gameplay elements : As in my previous projects, I programmed all gameplay elements such as buttons, pressure plates, cubes, doors, pistons, weight modifiers and anti-modifier barriers. The main challenge was allowing weight modifiers to physically attach to multiple level design elements to alter their properties.

• Cinematics and cameras : I learned how to create cinematics using Unity’s "Timeline" tool, used for level transitions as well as for the intro and the ending. I also developed a system allowing the camera target to change, helping to showcase level design and puzzles through smart camera movements.

• Reusing previous learnings : This project allowed me to apply my knowledge of inheritance polymorphism and overloading, the use of "Managers", and the separation of scripts by responsibility, improving code clarity and easing maintenance.
Amelioration_Text:
With more time, I would have approached certain aspects differently. First, I would have reworked the verticality handling of the controller to make it more fluid and responsive. Currently, the hand needs to build momentum to rise, which can frustrate players. A possible solution would have been to use an instantaneous force to make the movement more direct. Regarding the intro and ending cinematics, using Timeline was not ideal, as it does not natively allow skipping sections with a single click. Collaboration with the other programmers could also have been more efficient. Having never delegated tasks before, I had difficulties trusting and assigning work to the tech artists. A simple upfront task distribution would have allowed a better workload balance and significant time savings.

Despite this, the project taught me a great deal, whether about teamwork, physics, cinematics, or tool creation.
